cards.title: OAuth2 Core Concepts and Roles
cards.content:
Understanding OAuth 2.0 Roles

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that enables third-party applications to obtain limited access to an HTTP service.

  • Resource Owner: The user who grants access to a protected resource.
  • Client: The application making protected resource requests on behalf of the resource owner.
  • Resource Server: The server hosting the protected resources (e.g., your Spring Boot REST API).
  • Authorization Server: The server issuing access tokens to the client after successfully authenticating the resource owner.

content.question: In a Spring Boot application acting as a REST API protecting user profiles, what OAuth2 role does the Spring Boot application serve?

cards.title: Authorization Code Grant Flow with PKCE
cards.content:
Authorization Code Flow with PKCE

The standard flow for modern web applications and mobile clients:

  1. Client Initiates: Directs browser to Authorization Server with a Code Challenge (PKCE).
  2. User Authenticates: User logs in and consents to permissions (scopes).
  3. Authorization Code Issued: Authorization Server redirects back to Client with a temporary code.
  4. Token Exchange: Client sends the code along with Code Verifier to `/oauth2/token`.
  5. JWT Issued: Authorization Server validates parameters and returns Access & Refresh Tokens.

content.instruction: Arrange the steps of the Authorization Code Flow in correct order:

items.text: Client redirects user to Authorization Server authorization endpoint
Authorization Server redirects back to Client with authorization code
Client exchanges authorization code for Access Token at token endpoint
Client uses Access Token to request protected endpoints on Resource Server

cards.title: Configuring Spring Boot Resource Server
cards.content:
Configuring Spring Boot as a Resource Server

Add the Maven dependency:

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server</artifactId>
</dependency>

Configure application properties to point to the Issuer URI (e.g., Keycloak, Okta, Auth0):

spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri=https://auth.example.com/realms/demo

cards.title: Enforcing Scopes and Roles with Method Security
cards.content:
Scope and Authority Mapping

OAuth2 scopes present in a JWT payload (e.g. "scope": "read write") are automatically converted into Spring Security granted authorities prefixed with SCOPE_.

Enable method security with @EnableMethodSecurity and annotate controller methods:

@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_read')")
@GetMapping("/api/orders")
public List<Order> getOrders() {
    return orderService.findAll();
}

cards.title: Making Authenticated Calls with WebClient
cards.content:
Using OAuth2 Authorized Client with WebClient

When your Spring application acts as an OAuth2 Client invoking downstream microservices, configure ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction on WebClient.

@Bean
public WebClient webClient(OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager authorizedClientManager) {
    ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction filter =
        new ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction(authorizedClientManager);
    return WebClient.builder()
        .apply(filter.oauth2Configuration())
        .build();
}

content.question: How does a Spring Boot Resource Server verify the signature of an incoming JWT without keeping private keys locally?

options.text: By calling the Authorization Server on every single HTTP request
By downloading and caching public keys from the issuer's JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) URI
By decrypting the token using a shared symmetric database key
JWT signatures are not verified by Resource Servers, only by gateways
